why_this_tool: Debezium reads the database's own commit log and ships an outbox event router, so one tool lets you practise log based capture, outbox routing and rebuilding derived data on a laptop.
alternatives: Polling outbox publisher in the application (simple, but adds latency and load, and ordering is harder to guarantee); Kafka Connect JDBC source (query based, misses deletes and intermediate states); Maxwell or Canal (MySQL binlog only); DynamoDB Streams (managed change stream tied to one cloud database); PostgreSQL logical replication consumed directly (no connector framework, you write offset handling yourself).

setup.do: Read what Debezium is and sketch the pipeline you will build: PostgreSQL, Kafka, Kafka Connect with Debezium, and one consumer.
setup.done_when: You have a one-page diagram naming each container and the direction the data flows.
setup.why: A clear picture of the moving parts makes every later step easier to debug. It also fixes where the log, the connector and the topics sit.

setup.do: Install a container runtime and start Kafka plus a Kafka Connect container with the Debezium connector plugins on its plugin path.
setup.done_when: The Connect REST interface lists the Debezium PostgreSQL connector class among its installed plugins.

setup.do: Start a PostgreSQL container with logical WAL level and decide to use the built-in pgoutput plugin.
setup.done_when: A query of the WAL level setting returns logical and the database accepts connections from the Connect container.

setup.why: Logical decoding is what exposes committed changes to Debezium. The pgoutput plugin needs no extra installation in the database.

setup.done_when: You can state, for your stack, who creates the change topics and with what partition count and cleanup policy.

setup.why: Topic settings decide ordering and how long history is kept. Both matter once the log is treated as the source of truth.

steps.do: Run your first PostgreSQL connector against a small orders table that already holds a few rows, and watch the initial snapshot.
steps.done_when: A topic for the orders table exists and holds one read event per existing row.

steps.why: The snapshot shows how Debezium gets a consistent starting point before it follows the log. This is the first run every team does.

steps.do: Run an insert, an update and a delete on the orders table and query the topic to read the three streamed change events.
steps.done_when: You see three new events in commit order, each with an operation type, before and after state, and a log position.

steps.why: This is log based change data capture in action: committed changes arrive in commit order without the application publishing anything.

steps.do: Compare the architecture of the CockroachDB connector with your running PostgreSQL connector, mapping source log, connector task, topic, event key, event value and offsets in both.
steps.done_when: You have a two-column table that names the equivalent of each object for both connectors.

steps.why: The same object model recurs in every Debezium connector. Seeing it against a second database separates the concepts from PostgreSQL details.

steps.do: Run the MySQL connector against a local MySQL container with the same orders table and compare how it persists schema history with what the PostgreSQL connector does.
steps.done_when: You can show the schema history topic for MySQL and explain why the PostgreSQL connector has no such topic.

source.title: Debezium connector for MySQL :: Debezium Documentation

steps.why: Binlog capture needs a persisted schema history topic to interpret old log entries, where logical decoding does not. The difference affects how you operate and recover each connector.

steps.do: Reproduce the dual write problem with a script that commits an order row and then publishes to Kafka as a separate write, kill it between the two, then write down the outbox message that should replace the second write.
steps.done_when: You have one order in the database with no matching Kafka message, and a written outbox message with id, aggregate type, aggregate id, type and payload.
steps.why: Seeing the database and the topic disagree makes the failure concrete. The example message shows what must instead travel inside the transaction.

steps.do: Create the outbox table with the expected columns and change the script to insert the order row and the outbox row in one local transaction.
steps.done_when: Killing the script at any point never leaves an order without an outbox row or an outbox row without an order.
steps.why: The transactional outbox table makes the business change and the event atomic. A crash now loses both or neither.

steps.do: Configure the outbox event router transformation on a connector that captures only the outbox table, and run the script again.
steps.done_when: An order event topic receives messages whose key is the order id and whose value is only the payload.
steps.why: The router turns raw outbox row changes into clean domain events, routed to a topic per aggregate type and keyed by aggregate id. This preserves per-aggregate ordering.

steps.do: Run the Debezium JDBC sink in upsert mode from the routed topic into a second database, then restart the Connect worker mid-stream to force redelivery.
steps.done_when: After the restart the target table has exactly one row per order, with no duplicates and no errors in the sink status.

steps.why: Delivery is at least once, so a safe consumer must be idempotent. Upserts keyed on the primary key make replays harmless.

steps.do: Enable signaling, drop the derived orders table in the second database and trigger an incremental snapshot of the source table to rebuild it while streaming continues.
steps.done_when: The derived table is repopulated to match the source row count while new live changes keep arriving.

steps.why: Derived data is disposable when the log and the source remain the truth. Rebuilding on demand without stopping capture is how teams repair or add downstream views.

steps.do: Read how the Oracle connector mines from a downstream mining database; this needs a licensed database setup, so use your local PostgreSQL replication slot as the closest substitute and note the parallels.
steps.done_when: You can explain in three sentences where the log is read in that topology and what load it removes from the primary.

steps.why: Promoting capture off the primary onto a dedicated log reader is a common step before production. It shows how the capture path is moved without changing the events.

steps.do: Package a pinned Connect image that includes the scripting libraries for content-based routing, keep connector configurations as files in version control, and recreate the whole stack from scratch with a routing rule applied.
steps.done_when: A fresh checkout brings the stack up with one command and events matching your expression land in the alternate topic.
steps.why: A pinned image plus configuration in files makes the pipeline reproducible in CI and on any laptop. Content-based routing only works when its extra libraries are baked in.

steps.do: Configure a dedicated least-privilege replication role for the connector, switch the connector to it, and rerun the outbox flow end to end.
steps.done_when: The connector status is running under the restricted role and a new order still produces exactly one routed event and one derived row.

steps.why: Production databases do not hand superuser credentials to a connector. Running with only replication and select privileges is the baseline for a production-like setup.
